settings.description: A visual field guide to Atlantic coves, rock edges, and the marks that water leaves behind.

settings.title: Three ways to read a waterline
settings.subtitle: PHOTO PLATES
settings.description: Open a photograph for a closer look. Each caption starts with something visible in the frame.

gallery_image_copy.title: Sheltered cove
gallery_image_copy.caption: The curve of the headland partly encloses the water. Compare the sheltered inside edge with the opening toward the sea.
gallery_image_copy.alt: Ochre cliffs curve around Atlantic water in sunlight.

gallery_image_copy.title: Isolated rock stacks
gallery_image_copy.caption: The silhouettes make the gaps between the stacks easy to see. Compare how much of each rock meets the water.
gallery_image_copy.alt: Tall sea stacks are silhouetted offshore in warm evening light.

gallery_image_copy.title: A salt-flat margin
gallery_image_copy.caption: Compare this inland waterline with the coastal plates. Trace the pale edges and distinguish them from the colours reflected in the still water.
gallery_image_copy.alt: Pale rims edge still water that reflects mountains and a pink sky.

settings.title: Keep a field notebook
settings.subtitle: ON THE SHORE
settings.description: A simple record lets you compare observations across viewpoints and visits.

items.title: Describe the edge
items.description: Sketch where water meets land. Note what is continuous, where the edge breaks, and which details disappear into shadow.

items.title: Keep the conditions
items.description: Write down what you can see of wind, waves, visibility, and recent wetting alongside your sketch.

items.title: Return to one viewpoint
items.description: Repeat the same view from a safe place and compare waterlines, foam, and exposed surfaces.

settings.title: Match a clue to a note
settings.subtitle: FIELD REFERENCE
settings.description: Use this checklist to record what you see and mark what needs a second look.

static_rows.cells: Dark rock band|Where it begins and ends|Water, shade, and growth can all change colour.
Foam streak|Direction and how long it lasts|A single streak gives only a momentary view of surface motion.
Loose wrack line|Material and height above water|An older deposit can remain after the water recedes.

tabs.tab_title: Can a photo tell me the tide stage?
tabs.tab_content: A single photo rarely gives enough context. Compare it with time-stamped views from the same place and the relevant local tide record.

tabs.tab_title: What belongs in the first notebook entry?
tabs.tab_content: Record the viewpoint and conditions first. Add one sketch and a sentence that distinguishes your visible observation from a possible explanation.

tabs.tab_title: Where should I take a shoreline photo?
tabs.tab_content: Use a marked path or established viewpoint. Keep away from unstable cliff edges and leave low-lying areas where water could cut off your return.

settings.description: Choose a plate and start your own shoreline note.
